title: China's murals stayed crimson for two thousand years. The secret was blood, not pigment.
dek: The Zuojiang Huashan (左江花山) rock paintings have retained vivid red for two thousand years, with scientific analysis revealing that their pigment used lime mortar mixed with blood as a binder—some blood from postpartum women, possibly reflecting ritual significance in a matriarchal society.
why: This episode is a cross-topic news roundup without a unified narrative, but shipwreck salvage, rock-painting chemical analysis, vampire graves, and other stories each bring solid new evidence and figures.
who: Anyone curious about archaeology news, artifact salvage, and art history gossip; this works well as a weekly dose of obscure history.

points.h: Pre-Columbian trade between Mississippi and Mesoamerica is evidenced by cacao DNA in Georgia
points.body: Pottery sherds from 11th-century Etowah Mounds in Georgia contained cacao biomarkers and DNA, initially thought to be yupon holly tea. Subsequent DNA testing confirmed cacao from at least two sherds. The nearest known cacao source was southern Mexico, indicating undocumented long-distance trade between Mississippi culture and Mesoamerica.

points.h: A sealed Guinness recovered from an 1864 wreck proved disappointingly mundane
points.body: Divers found a sealed bottle of Guinness Foreign Extra Stout in the Mondoro wreck, which sank in the English Channel in 1864. Researchers prepared both safety analysis and yeast DNA sequencing—involving Leuven University and Guinness Archives—to potentially recreate the 19th-century recipe. When results arrived during recording, the safety report proved anticlimactic.

points.h: Shackleton's Quest wreck reveals structural details in first close-up photographs
points.body: Sonar located Shackleton's Quest wreck in 2024. Canada's Royal Geographic Society and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution used deep-submergence vehicle Alvin—famous for reaching the Titanic—to capture the first close-up images. Photos show the bow, deck, portholes, and collapsed main mast, now encrusted with soft coral. The same project captured first high-resolution images of Scott's final ship, Terra Nova.

points.h: Batavia's building stones reveal complex colonial supply chains across European quarries
points.body: The 1629 Batavia carried stone and brick originally destined for the Dutch East India Company headquarters in Jakarta. These materials were long assumed to come from a single quarry. Zircon microanalysis revealed they came from at least two different German quarries, demonstrating the complexity of colonial supply systems that coordinated materials from multiple sources.

points.h: A medieval German cellar preserves an intact ship hull as ceiling
points.body: A 1244 cellar in Constance, Germany, has a nearly intact ship hull spanning over 25 square meters as its ceiling, with 19 wooden hull planks and connecting dowels still in place. Medieval convention required dismantling salvaged ships before reusing them as building materials. This entire hull was embedded instead, preserving structural details and repair marks without requiring underwater study.

points.h: Blood mixed into lime mortar explains two millennia of vivid color in rock paintings
points.body: The Zuojiang Huashan rock paintings, spread across 260 kilometers of cliffs, have maintained vivid red color for over two thousand years despite typhoons and sun exposure. Electron microscopy of stone flakes revealed the pigment used iron-oxide red clay particles locked in place by lime-sand mortar mixed with blood as binder. Blood serum analysis identified postpartum women's blood—possibly reflecting rituals from a matriarchal society—alongside animal blood.

points.h: Australia's largest rainbow serpent paintings were created after European colonization, not before
points.body: Griffith University researchers, collaborating with Amurdag traditional custodians, studied 165 rock-art sites across Australia's Northern Territory. Due to pigment composition and layer overlap, most paintings could not be carbon-dated. Combining these findings with oral tradition, researchers determined that the largest rainbow serpent and ancestor-figure murals were created after European arrival—interpreted as indigenous responses to colonization, reasserting cultural control through symbols of creation and destruction.

points.h: A Polish grave shows signs of attempted exhumation and body disruption
points.body: A 2022 Polish grave contained a girl aged 17 to 19 with an iron sickle on her neck and padlock on her left big toe—local anti-vampire measures. Silk hat remains indicate wealth. Soil disturbance revealed earlier exhumation attempts while the body was still decomposing, likely during the same period when the sickle and padlock were placed. Carbon dating places her death between 1620 and 1674; isotope analysis shows prior malnutrition.
